title: Other Christians
hook: Methodists, Baptists, Pentecostals and others in dialogue with Catholics

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lutherans and Catholics in Lund: thanksgiving, repentance and commitment. Your line was from conflict to communion.

A Saturday morning on a main street. A Methodist church with a sign out front about a pancake breakfast. A Baptist church with a baptism pool behind the pulpit. A storefront Pentecostal church where the singing spills out onto the sidewalk. A Catholic parish with confessions until noon. Four doors, four ways of worshiping, and Catholics walking past all of them. What does the Catholic Church say about the people behind those other doors?
screen: `FOUR DOORS ON ONE STREET.` → `FOUR WAYS OF WORSHIPING.` → `WHO IS BEHIND THE OTHER DOORS?`

segments.voice: Day three hundred twenty gave you the short answer; here's the longer one. The council's decree on ecumenism teaches that those who believe in Christ and have been properly baptized are in a real, though imperfect, communion with the Catholic Church. They are rightly called Christians, it says, and rightly accepted by Catholics as brothers in the Lord. Brothers is the council's word. Why does baptism matter so much? In the Douay-Rheims, Paul writes to the Ephesians: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism." The Catholic Church recognizes baptism given in other churches with water in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. So a Catholic and a Baptist, whatever they disagree about, are already joined by one baptism. Then the conversations. Beyond Anglicans and Lutherans, the Catholic Church holds formal dialogues with Methodists, with Baptists, with Pentecostals and with others, some old, some newer, about grace, Scripture, the Spirit, holiness and mission. Methodists bring their founder John Wesley, who once preached that even when Christians can't think alike, they might still love alike. Pentecostals bring their experience of the Spirit, which the Catholic charismatic renewal also prizes. Last, honesty. These dialogues don't erase real differences, about the sacraments, the pope, Mary, how churches are led. They name them. But the starting point isn't suspicion. It's a family resemblance: one baptism, one Lord, and the council's word, brothers.
screen: `A REAL, THOUGH IMPERFECT, COMMUNION.` · `ONE LORD, ONE FAITH, ONE BAPTISM.` · `METHODISTS, BAPTISTS, PENTECOSTALS.` · `DIFFERENCES NAMED, NOT ERASED.` · then, large: `BROTHERS IN THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Think of one Christian tradition you know little about, Methodist, Baptist, Pentecostal, Mennonite, Orthodox, and picture the people walking into one of their churches this Sunday. If you pray, pray for them as the council describes them, brothers and sisters in Christ. If you don't, hold them in mind with goodwill and a little curiosity.
Other Christians. Baptized believers in Christ in other churches, whom the council calls brothers in the Lord. Today's word.
Your line: brothers and sisters in Christ. Behind those other doors, family. Rest well.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church holds official dialogues with a number of Christian communities, including Methodists, Baptists and Pentecostals, and in some towns local churches of different traditions share prayer services and service projects.

chat.says: Does the Catholic Church think I'm really a Christian, even though I'm Methodist?
options: Yes. The council says the baptized in other churches are rightly called Christians, brothers in the Lord.
Only once you're confirmed in a Catholic parish; until then you'd count as a seeker.
Yes, because the Church says no real differences are left between the churches.

notes: Unitatis Redintegratio 3 paraphrased: those who believe in Christ and have been truly (properly) baptized are in communion with the Catholic Church even though this communion is imperfect; justified by faith in baptism, they are incorporated into Christ; they have a right to be called Christians and are accepted as brothers by the children of the Catholic Church.
